## Why This Is Asked
Tests non-branching bit-twiddling across a 128-bit value. The triple overlap trick scales beyond 64 bits.

## Key Concepts
- Wide integer bit shifts with zero fill
- Bitwise AND to intersect bit positions
- Non-branching return logic for 0/1 result

## Code Example
```c
unsigned hasThreeConsecutiveOnes128(uint128 x){
  uint128 t = x & (x>>1) & (x>>2);
  return t != 0;
}
```

- Could you return the starting index of the first triplet if present?

Tests precise bitfield extraction in arbitrary alignments, a common requirement in parsers and low-level codecs. No loops or branches; relies on safe shifts and masks.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to apply simple bit-tricks succinctly and reason about edge cases without loops. It also shows understanding of bitwise adjacency relationships across 64 bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise AND and right shift
- Detecting pattern overlap without branching
- Constant-time evaluation on fixed width integers

## Code Example

```javascript
function hasConsecutiveOnes(n) {
  // n treated as a 64-bit value; bitwise ops apply to 32-bit in JS
  return (n & (n >>> 1)) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend to count how many adjacent pairs exist?
- How would you test correctness with edge inputs like all zeros, all ones, alternating patterns?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of 128-bit shifts, wrap-around logic, and edge cases where n==0. Requires a clean, branch-minimal implementation without loops.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation across 128 bits
- Handling edge cases safely (n==0, 128-n)
- Avoiding undefined shifts across boundary bits

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, uint8 n) {
  n &= 127;
  if (n == 0) return x;
  return (x << n) | (x >> (128 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a language without 128-bit integers?
- How would compiler optimizations affect this implementation in real code?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests candidates' knowledge of bit-twiddling techniques and SWAR parallelism on 128-bit values without branches or loops. It demonstrates understanding of low-level bit manipulation essential for performance-critical code, cryptographic implementations, and hardware-level programming.

## Key Concepts
- **SWAR (SIMD Within A Register)**: A technique for parallel bit manipulation across multiple fields within a single register, treating the register as a vector of smaller data elements
- **Three-pass reversal algorithm**: Uses masks 0x55, 0x33, and 0x0F to progressively reverse bits within each byte by swapping adjacent bits, then adjacent 2-bit pairs, then adjacent nibbles
